The three algorithms

One free-space idea, three edit rules.

Every state asks whether the current pair (πᵢ, σⱼ) is within δ. The allowed edits decide what happens when it is not.

Delete rows

Deletion only

When the current σ vertex is too far away, delete it. Compatible cells use the three ordinary discrete Fréchet predecessors.

far:  D[i,j] = 1 + D[i,j−1]
near: min(D[i,j−1],
          D[i−1,j], D[i−1,j−1])
O(mn)time
Bridge columns

Insertion only

An inserted point may cover a whole suffix of π if that suffix fits in a radius-δ ball. μ(i) marks the earliest possible start.

insert(i,j) = 1 + min I[k−1,j]
                 μ(i) ≤ k ≤ i
O(m² + mn)MEB preprocessing + DP
Choose the cheaper repair

Insertion + deletion

At an incompatible pair, either remove σⱼ or insert a point covering a valid π block. Compatible cells also keep the three no-cost moves.

far: min(1 + B[i,j−1],
         insert(i,j))
O(m² + mn)time

Why minimum enclosing balls?

One inserted point can stand in for several reference vertices.

If πₖ…πᵢ all fit inside a closed ball of radius δ, the ball’s center is a legal inserted vertex matched to that entire block. It need not be an existing input point.

Presentation guide

A five-minute live explanation.

Use the “repair both” preset and walk from geometry to recurrence to complexity.

  1. 1
    Set the objective

    π is fixed. We edit σ until their strong discrete Fréchet distance is at most δ.

  2. 2
    Show the outlier

    The distant cyan point makes the ordinary distance large; deletion removes its free-space row.

  3. 3
    Show the gap

    Undersampling creates a horizontal gap. An inserted MEB center bridges a whole π block.

  4. 4
    Compare restrictions

    Deletion-only and insertion-only can be infeasible. The combined method chooses both types.

  5. 5
    Land the complexity

    Monotone μ values plus a minimum queue reduce each DP column to linear time.
